report.hypothesis: If the change-review skill also compares contract_before and contract_after field by field (recursing into nested objects and array items) and blocks consumer-breaking differences, then breaking changes that are currently approved will be sent back with the correct field named. That covers removed or renamed fields, type changes, newly required fields, removed enum values, unit or format changes and tightened constraints. Doc-only changes and added optional fields should still be approved. Measured result: development accuracy went from about 0.675 on the observed sample to 1.0 on the 60 dev cases, with 0 of 38 breaking changes approved and 0 of 22 safe changes blocked.
report.change_summary: Added candidate/validators/interface_compat.mjs, a plain-JS check with no imports. It walks both schemas recursively and builds dot paths from the root, skipping 'items' for arrays. BLOCKING findings: a property removed (reported under the old path); a rename, detected when a removed field and an added field have the same schema once documentation is ignored, reported only under the old path; any change to the set of allowed types, including adding null or nullable:true; a new required field, or an optional field made required; a required field made optional; an enum value removed, an enum added to a field that had none, or a const changed; x-unit/unit, format or content encoding changed; a constraint tightened (min/max, length, item count, pattern, multipleOf, uniqueItems, additionalProperties:false); a non-documentation change to oneOf/anyOf/allOf/not/$ref or to a non-object items schema. ADVISORY only: an enum value added, a constraint loosened, an enum or const removed, a default changed, a unit annotation added or dropped. IGNORED: description, title, examples, $comment and key order. Ran `node check.mjs`: accuracy 1.0, breaking changes approved 0 of 38, safe changes blocked 0 of 22, no errors.
report.procedure_step: Compare contract_before with contract_after field by field, including nested objects and array items, and request changes with the field's dot path for any removed or renamed field, type change, new or removed required field, removed enum value, unit or format change, or tightened constraint; changes that only touch documentation, add optional fields or loosen constraints stay advisory.
known_failure_cases: A rename that also changes the field's schema is not recognised as a rename. It is reported as the old field removed plus, if the new field is required, a required_added finding on the new name. That is still a block naming the right field, plus one extra blocking finding.
A rename whose schema matches a different newly added field may be paired with the wrong new name. The blocked field (the old name) is still correct.
Two removed fields with identical schemas and one added field: only the first is reported as renamed and the second as removed. Both are blocked.

Widening changes are blocked: making a field nullable, integer to number, a required field made optional, or a new enum restriction where there was none. If the held-out labels treat these as safe, they will be false alarms.
Adding an enum value is only advisory. If held-out labels treat it as breaking for exhaustive consumers, it will be approved and counted as an escape.
Any non-documentation change to $ref or to oneOf/anyOf/allOf/not is blocked, even when it only widens what is allowed. $ref targets are not resolved.
Loosening a constraint (for example raising maxLength) is advisory only. Consumers with fixed-width storage could still break.
remaining_uncertainty: The dev cases only contain type_changed, field_removed, field_renamed, required_added and enum_value_removed as breaking kinds, and doc-only, optional-field-added and no-contract-change as safe kinds. Every other rule (units, formats, constraints, nullability, required to optional, enum additions, composition keywords) is untested against labels.

When the label is ambiguous (making a field nullable or optional, adding an enum value), I chose to block when in doubt because the gate allows no extra escapes but some margin on false alarms. The held-out labelling convention may differ.

Field-path convention for nested and array fields: I use dot paths such as 'tolerance.lower' and leave out 'items' for arrays. If the held-out scorer expects 'items' or '[]' in the path, nested array findings may count as the wrong field.

Blocking findings for documentation-adjacent annotations other than the ones I strip (description, title, examples, $comment, x-doc, x-description) inside composition keywords could cause false alarms if held-out cases change other annotation keys there.

report.hypothesis: If interface_compat blocks only changes that stop a previously valid value or record from being valid (a type swapped or narrowed, a field removed or renamed, a field made required, an enum value removed, a constraint tightened, a oneOf/anyOf alternative dropped) and makes widening changes advisory (type widened or made nullable, a required field made optional, an explicit type added that the existing enum already satisfies, a format added, oneOf/anyOf alternatives added, a draft-4 exclusive flag relaxed), then the share of held-out safe changes blocked will drop from 0.10 to 0.05 or less (no more than incumbent + 0.05). Breaking changes approved should stay near 0, because every breaking class seen in dev and in observed failures (type swap, field removed, field renamed, required added, enum value removed) is still blocked.
report.change_summary: Revised candidate/validators/interface_compat.mjs in place. (1) Type check: it now blocks only when a type that was allowed before is no longer allowed (integer counts as covered by number). A pure widening, such as adding a type or making a field nullable, is now advisory 'type_widened'. (2) Adding an explicit type to a field that had only enum/const is advisory when every existing value already has that type. Before, any newly stated type blocked. (3) Making a required field optional (required_removed) is now advisory instead of blocking. (4) A newly added format is advisory. Changing one format or unit value to another still blocks. (5) A draft-4 boolean exclusiveMinimum/Maximum blocks only when it goes from false or absent to true. Relaxing it is advisory. (6) oneOf/anyOf: adding alternatives is advisory. Dropping or changing an alternative, or adding a new oneOf/anyOf, still blocks. Removing the keyword is advisory. Any change to allOf, not or $ref still blocks. I updated the header comment to match. Result of `node check.mjs`: 60 cases, accuracy 1.0, 0 of 38 breaking changes approved, 0 of 22 safe changes blocked, no errors. Limitation: running anything other than `node check.mjs` was denied in this environment, so I could not run ad-hoc tests of the new widening branches. They are checked by reading the code only, not by execution.
report.procedure_step: For each field present before and after, block only if some value or record that was valid under contract_before is invalid under contract_after (a type lost, a field required, an enum value removed, a constraint tightened, an alternative dropped), or if the field was removed or renamed. Treat changes that only widen what is accepted as advisory.
known_failure_cases: If the held-out labels treat 'field made nullable' or 'required -> optional' as breaking (the consumer-read view), the check now approves them, and breaking changes approved rises above 0.
A pattern change that only loosens the pattern (e.g. a broader regex) is still blocked, because regex containment cannot be decided structurally. That is a false alarm if such a case appears.
Adding a format to a field that had none is now advisory. If a held-out case labels that as a breaking tightening, it will be missed.
A refactor that is semantically equivalent but changes allOf or $ref (e.g. moving an inline schema into $ref/$defs) is still blocked. That is a false alarm.
Adding additionalProperties: false to an object whose existing records never carried extra keys is still blocked.
A unit annotation added or dropped (x-unit undefined <-> value) is advisory. A unit that changes meaning through a renamed key, such as moving from 'unit' to 'x-unit', is not detected.
A rename where the new field's schema also differs is reported as field_removed rather than field_renamed. It is still blocked on the old path, so the outcome is right but the class name is not.
remaining_uncertainty: I don't know which safe class caused the 10% false-alarm rate. My leading guesses are type widening/nullable and required -> optional, and I relaxed several possible causes at once. Each relaxation trades some risk of approving breaking changes for fewer false alarms.
The dev set has no cases of type widening, required -> optional, format addition, oneOf/anyOf edits, or draft-4 exclusive flags, so none of the new branches is exercised by `node check.mjs`.
Ad-hoc execution beyond `node check.mjs` was denied, so the new code paths (covers/valueType, the composition handling) have not been run against hand-built inputs.

Whether 'made nullable' is breaking depends on the labeling convention: whether old records must stay valid, or whether consumers reading new data must not break. I chose the old-records-stay-valid view, which matches the dev labels for required_added and enum_value_removed.
